extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, government science administrators, university leaders and research foundation trustees
extracted.subtask_description: Recommendations and operational principles for government support of university scientific research, including forms of aid (matching grants, discretionary grants, fellowships, capital facilities) and reforms to government research administration and civil service rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of funds: support significant research emphasizing pure science
rubrics_metrics.description: The funds supplied to the universities should be used for the support of significant research with special emphasis on the universities’ position as the chief contributor to pure science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants should target fundamental research; preserve universities’ leading role in pure science rather than directing them toward narrowly applied project work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assure competent and adequately trained personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: In making grants the board should assure itself that the university has competent and adequately trained personnel to guide the studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before awarding funds, the board must satisfy itself of institutional personnel quality; personnel capacity is a condition of grant eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid external control of university internal policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants to universities or to men working in universities must be made in such a way as to avoid control of the internal policy of the university, so that the university and not the board will have full responsibility for the administration of the grant after it is once made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure funding to minimize board interference; preserve academic freedom and institutional autonomy once funds are granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve general research level across institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A constant effort should be made to improve the general research level in institutions of higher education throughout the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding programs should include explicit aims to raise research capability beyond a few elite universities and promote broader geographic and institutional distribution of research activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve variety and decentralization in scientific work
rubrics_metrics.description: Devising ways and means of allocating funds in large measure without determining what particular problems are to be worked on and who is to carry them out; the principle of variety and decentralization of control is nowhere more important than in scientific work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow latitude to university administrators and faculties to choose research directions; avoid centralized prescription of specific problems or personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomous board freedom within broad principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A largely autonomous board with a staff of men trained in science is the most appropriate agency for carrying on this phase of the Government’s responsibility for scientific progress; such a board should be free to formulate its own rules as long as these do not transgress certain broad general principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create an autonomous trustee board with scientific staff; restrict only by high-level principles (academic freedom, personnel competence, broad objectives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching grants to accredited institutions (automatic, contingent on bookkeeping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research funds be made available to accredited universities, colleges, and engineering schools on a matching basis, and in a manner that will be virtually automatic; contingent upon satisfying the administrating board that certain clearly stated requirements, largely of a technical bookkeeping nature have been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matches should be for fluid research purposes (not department/person-specific), be predictable annual appropriations, and require only administrative/accounting compliance; Government matches dollar-for-dollar (or similar simple formula).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and practical issues of matching grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Matching grants leave recipients freedom in selecting programs/personnel, encourage local support, size the grant to institutional capacity, and free the board from intensive project-by-project adjudication; practical problems include distinguishing research costs from teaching costs in nonuniform university accounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use matching grants to leverage local support and reduce central review load, but establish clear accounting standards and exclude funds tied to industrial contracts that would yield exclusive industrial property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary grants to spread research and support special projects
rubrics_metrics.description: The board of trustees be empowered to expend a substantial part of its funds on a discretionary basis, either as grants-in-aid for promising special projects or in the provision of large and expensive capital facilities, to help spread the research spirit and raise research practice in many colleges and engineering schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve discretionary funds to support institutions that cannot benefit adequately from matching grants and to promote geographic/institutional balance of research activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants‑in‑aid: size, duration, and focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants-in-aid range from small one-year awards to large multi-year appropriations; a government foundation with large resources should abstain from frittering efforts on many small transient projects and instead prefer substantial, stable multi-year support for promising projects and under-resourced institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor multi-year, sizable awards for capacity-building and promising research rather than numerous small short-term grants; use to achieve balance of research activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants for capital facilities and shared expensive equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Government could aid research by making large and highly expensive pieces of equipment and capital facilities available to universities, with provisions that they should be used cooperatively by other institutions in the region and adapted to local circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support construction/purchase of cyclotrons, ultracentrifuges, computing centers, etc., with regional cooperative use policies; detailed management plans will be needed to govern sharing and placement to stimulate less-favored areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑doctoral research fellowships to recruit and train researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: A program of post-doctoral fellowships to aid research workers who have recently received advanced degrees and wish additional years to establish themselves before taking heavy teaching duties; many fellows work at institutions other than where they received their degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use postdoctoral fellowships to (1) reintegrate veterans or those whose training was interrupted, (2) broaden training via mobility between institutions, and (3) supply immediate research assistance in universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior research fellowships to support mature investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Fellowships large enough to meet the salaries of advanced academic personnel for periods of intensive research at their own or other institutions; accompanied grants should cover the use of research facilities at the selected institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use senior fellowships to reduce immobility, stimulate exchange of distinguished workers, enable intensive research free of routine duties, and attract experienced scientists from industry/government into university research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient laboratory assistance and supplementary funds
rubrics_metrics.description: It is vitally important that sufficient laboratory assistance, materials, apparatus, clerical and manual aid be provided for university staff members undertaking research; it is anomalous to hire first-class scientists and fail to provide supplementary funds necessary for productive research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure budgets include direct operating costs (apparatus, materials, technical assistance) so senior scientists are not used for shop work; match industrial practice of supporting research staff with adequate assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark adequate supplementary research expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: Prewar university departments spent roughly 10–40 cents per salary dollar on direct research operating costs (typical 15–20 cents), whereas industrial labs spent much more (often $1–$3 per salary dollar); steps must be taken to bring university supplementary research expenditures more into line with best practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to raise university per‑salary-dollar direct research expenditures substantially above historical low university levels to achieve economical and productive research comparable to industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid annual project-specific congressional appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee does not feel it desirable to supply these funds by a series of annual congressional appropriations for specific projects; such appropriations introduce evils into the university environment and endanger academic freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor institutional funding mechanisms (e.g., autonomous foundation) instead of project-by-project congressional control to encourage long-term projects and minimize external interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal/budgetary reform: appropriations for long‑term programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Current budgetary procedure provides funds on an annual basis yet only a small percentage of research can be planned or appraised on a 1-year basis; research programs should be assured in terms of their long-run objectives and funds guaranteed over required years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt lump-sum appropriations for broad programs with internal annual allocations rather than detailed annual justifications; make such procedures uniform across government scientific bureaus to permit flexibility and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable cooperative financial support from state/local/private agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be a relatively simple matter for any scientific bureau of the Government to accept funds from State or local governments, from non-profit research institutions, or from private industry, for cooperative scientific investigations that are in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove bureaucratic obstacles to accepting cooperative funds; encourage Federal support for research addressing more-than-local issues and stimulate research organizations in economically backward states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify fiscal regulations for purchase of scientific equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Government regulations regarding purchase of supplies and equipment (calls for bids, insistence on lowest-priced material) often hamper research programs by preventing acquisition of best quality scientific equipment and causing delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberalize procurement rules for scientific equipment to prioritize quality and timely acquisition over strict lowest-price bidding when appropriate to avoid intangible losses in research productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Service reform: separate classification for scientific/technical personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific and professional personnel in Government service are subject to the same system as clerical and custodial positions; separate and distinct procedures for recruiting and classifying scientific personnel are warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a separate Civil Service branch for scientific/technical positions to permit recruitment, classification, and promotion practices suited to technical needs while preserving merit safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrance requirements: require degree for scientific positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for entrance into scientific and professional positions should be approximately those maintained for comparable posts in universities and industries; requirement of a university or college degree for entrance into all scientific and professional services should be re-established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant exceptions only upon recommendation of qualified scientists; avoid lowering standards by granting military or other preference that results in unqualified appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment practices: expedite and permit interviews and student appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Government bureaus are handicapped competing with industry due to slow Civil Service processes; it should be permissible for government representatives to interview students, reduce delays between application and appointment, permit college seniors to be appointed effective on graduation, and use temporary student summer appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow faster hiring mechanisms and proactive recruiting to attract able young scientists while maintaining probationary and examination safeguards for promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary scales: make pay competitive and permit high nonadministrative salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Salary scales must be broadly commensurate with those of private institutions; Civil Service regulations should permit exceptionally qualified scientists to reach salaries (e.g., $9,000 or more) even if they do not have major administrative responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust promotion and salary structures to retain top scientific talent in government service, and permit directors' salaries as necessary to attract outstanding leadership (subject to congressional constraints).
